# The Tale of Mosspond and the Great Spring Stand

The sun hung low over Mosspond, painting the water orange as the tadpoles swirled into a tight circle around the largest lily pad. Old Rip, the oldest toad in the pond, sat on a mossy log, his warts glinting in the twilight.

“Listen close, little ones,” he croaked, “and I’ll tell you why our pond is the best place in all the wet world.”

You’ve all heard how we live here: no one croaks orders, no one demands you do what they say. When the algae beds need tending, the tadpoles who love sliding through the mud get to work. When the cattails need weaving into nets, the ones who like floating on their backs practice their knots. When the Spring Sifter needs a new reed filter, the beetles who crawl through the reeds step up to tie it on. No boss, no chief—just folks doing what they’re good at, because they care.

Last moon, a dry spell came. The water in the spring slowed to a trickle, and the Drain Dwellers showed up. They were crayfish and newts from the storm drain up the bank, their shells cracked and their bellies empty. “This spring is ours!” they snapped. “You’ll give us half your stored food, or we’ll block the spring forever.”

The tadpoles held their breath. What would we do? No one was in charge to tell us what to fight with, what to build, what to say. But then—something magic happened.

The youngest tadpoles zoomed off to gather smooth pebbles and thick cattail fibers. The water beetles scurried to the Glider Nets, the floating barriers strung between the red maple logs, and tightened their knots. The adult toads rolled over to the Spring Sifter, the reed-and-tin machine that filtered the spring water, and twisted its water wheel to spin faster.

When the Drain Dwellers marched down the shallow edge of the pond, they found something they didn’t expect: a wall of swirling water, pushed by the Spring Sifter’s wheel, blocking the spring’s mouth. The Glider Nets were strung tight across the shallow spots, their cattail fibers glinting like silver. The tadpoles were swarming around the nets, pushing small rocks to weigh them down. No one was yelling, no one was pointing—everyone just did what they knew how to do.

One of the Drain Dwellers, a young crayfish with a broken claw, peeked over the net. “You don’t have a leader,” he said, confused. “How do you all work together?”

Old Rip hopped over, his tongue flicking out to catch a mosquito. “We don’t need a leader,” he said. “We just need to remember that everyone’s got something to give. Some of us weave nets, some of us fix machines, some of us swim fast and scare away the big fish. When trouble comes, we all show up.”

The Drain Dwellers looked at each other. They told us they were scared—their drain was drying up, and they didn’t know how to get water for their own young. Old Rip nodded, and the tadpoles carried over jars of stored water. The beetles showed them how to build a small Spring Sifter from hollowed-out reeds and a tin can. No one made them stay, no one demanded they follow our ways—we just shared what we knew.

By the next full moon, the Drain Dwellers had their own small spring filter, and they brought back crayfish traps full of minnows to share with Mosspond.

The tadpoles swished their tails excitedly. Old Rip smiled. “That’s how it works here, little ones. No one owns the pond, no one tells you what to be. You just be the best tadpole you can be, and help the others when you can. That’s the best way to live.”

The tadpoles cheered, swirling faster in the water. They couldn’t wait to grow up, to build nets, to fix machines, to stand with their pond family.
